rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites reject faith like that of the verified believers of Yathrib, calling them mentally light; safah denotes lightness and thinness, as in the fabric metaphor and Dhu al-Rumma's line.
rows.anchor: والسفه الخفة والرقة الداعية إلى الخفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their secret insult was disclosed; corrupt judgment and shallow understanding belong to the hypocrites, who fail to recognize their folly because their hearts are encrusted.
rows.anchor: للرين الذي على قلوبهم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some identify the audience as Jewish hypocrites and take “the people” to mean ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām and Israelites who converted; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this restriction as unsupported.
rows.anchor: الآية نزلت في منافقي اليهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form liqaw derives from liqiyū, with the yāʾ dropped after the vowel was lightened; Ibn al-Sumayfa reads “lāqaw.”
rows.anchor: أصله لقيوا استثقلت الضمة على الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypocrites professed Islam before believers and showed disbelief in private; kinship clouded proof, while their public profession protected their lives and the Prophet refrained from killing them lest people say he killed his companions.
rows.anchor: دعه لا يتحدث الناس أن محمدا يقتل أصحابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When ʿUmar urged killing ʿAbd Allāh b. Ubayy after his “honorable” and “humiliated” remark, the Prophet told him to leave the man alive to avoid that public accusation.
rows.anchor: لئن رجعنا إلى المدينة ليخرجن الأعز منها الأذل

rows.speaker: أصحاب مالك
rows.claim: The Maliki position explains the Prophet's restraint despite knowing the hypocrites' general disbelief as a precedent that a judge does not rule from private knowledge; it cites the warning in 33:60–61 if they openly manifest hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: الحاكم لا يحكم بعلمه إذ لم يشهد على المنافقين

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He interprets the threat against hypocrites as applying when they openly declare their hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: معناه إذا هم أعلنوا النفاق

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik equates the hypocrite of the Prophet's era with the present-day zindīq and says a zindīq is executed on testimony without an opportunity to repent, since he conceals what would be repented of.
rows.anchor: النفاق في عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم هو الزندقة فينا اليوم

rows.speaker: إسماعيل القاضي
rows.claim: He says only Zayd b. Arqam testified against ʿAbd Allāh b. Ubayy and only ʿUmayr b. Saʿd against al-Jullās; two witnesses to either man's disbelief or hypocrisy would have led to execution.
rows.anchor: لم يشهد على عبد الله بن أبي إلا زيد بن أرقم وحده

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو محمد عبد الحق
rows.claim: He argues the testimony was not explicit proof of disbelief; rather, disbelief was inferred from the force of the words, making this stronger than the mere fact that one witness stood alone.
rows.anchor: اللفظ ليس بصريح كفر وإنما يفهم من قوته الكفر

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī says an accused zindīq who denies the charge, openly professes Islam, and disavows other religions is not to be killed; the Ahl al-Raʾy and al-Ṭabarī agree.
rows.anchor: السنة فيمن شهد عليه بالزندقة فجحد وأعلن بالإيمان

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأصحابه
rows.claim: They explain that outward Islam erased what preceded it, as it did for the Prophet's hypocrites; imposing harsher treatment on zindīqs conflicts with Qurʾān and Sunna and elevates witness testimony above God's testimony about hypocrites.
rows.anchor: ما يظهرونه يجب ما قبله فمن قال إن عقوبة الزنادقة أشد

rows.speaker: الشافعي وأبو حنيفة وابن حنبل وأهل الحديث
rows.claim: They say the Prophet was barred from killing hypocrites who outwardly professed Islam and prayed; the same rule applies to a zindīq.
rows.anchor: أن الله تعالى نهاه عن قتلهم إذا أظهروا الإيمان وصلوا

rows.speaker: ابن حنبل
rows.claim: He cites the report of ʿUbayd Allāh b. ʿAdī from an Anṣārī about a man accused of hypocrisy: the Prophet asked whether he testified to the two testimonies and prayed, then said these were people God forbade him to kill.
rows.anchor: أولئك الذين نهاني الله عنهم

rows.speaker: أهل الحديث
rows.claim: They also transmit the Prophet's hope that descendants of the hypocrites would believe in God, affirm the messengers, and devote worship sincerely to the Lord of all worlds.
rows.anchor: لعل الله سيخرج من أصلابهم من يؤمن بالله

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says legal judgments concern outward conduct, while God alone judges hidden states; the Prophet treated hypocrites as Muslims according to their profession, despite God's disclosure of their lying in 63:1.
rows.anchor: قد جعل الأحكام بين عباده على الظاهر

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو محمد
rows.claim: The Malikis answer that 63:1 rebukes anyone suspected of hypocrisy generally without identifying individuals; each could deny being its subject, so it did not expose a particular person's lie in a way that canceled his profession.
rows.anchor: لم تعين أشخاصهم وإنما جاء فيها توبيخ لكل مغموض عليه بالنفاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khala is normally joined to bi, but here ilā follows it because khala means “went away,” parallel to liqaw; al-Farazdaq's verse likewise uses a verb meaning to turn or depart.
rows.anchor: وصلت خلوا ب إلى وعرفها أن توصل بالباء

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī says khala bi-flān can mean to mock him, so the verse's ilā removes the possible ambiguity associated with bi.
rows.anchor: يقال خلوت بفلان بمعنى سخرت به

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some take ilā to mean maʿa (“with”); Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak and points ahead to 3:52 and 61:14.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا ضعف ويأتي بيانه إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say ilā substitutes for bi because particles can replace one another; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as weak and contrary to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh.
rows.anchor: وهذا ضعيف يأباه الخليل وسيبويه وغيرهما

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās interprets the hypocrites' satans as the leaders of disbelief.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس رضي الله عنه: «هم رؤساء الكفر»

rows.speaker: ابن الكلبي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Kalbī and others identify the satans as jinn; Ibn ʿAṭiyya regards that as unlikely in this context.
rows.anchor: هم شياطين الجن

rows.speaker: جمع من المفسرين
rows.claim: A group of commentators say the satans are soothsayers; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the term's sense of distance from faith and good can encompass all these groups and the hypocrites themselves.
rows.anchor: جمع من المفسرين: «هم الكهان»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We are only mocking” means they regard the believers whom they flatter by professing faith as objects of ridicule and contempt.
rows.anchor: نتخذ هؤلاء الذين نصانعهم بإظهار الإيمان هزوا

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh writes the hamza of mustahziʾūn with ḍamma over wāw; Abū ʿAlī reports his allowance of a softened hamza.
rows.anchor: ومذهب سيبويه رحمه الله أن تكون الهمزة مضمومة على الواو

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash reads mustahziyun by turning the hamza into a full yāʾ; Ibn Jinnī explains its ḍamma as recalling the original hamza, since Arabs dislike a yāʾ with ḍamma after kasra.
rows.anchor: أن تقلب الهمزة ياء قلبا صحيحا فيقرأ «مستهزيون»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most reciters follow Sībawayh's form; haziʾa and istahzaʾa are synonymous, like ʿajiba and istaʿjaba, and Aws b. Ḥajar's verse illustrates the latter form.
rows.anchor: وأكثر القراء على ما ذهب إليه سيبويه

rows.speaker: جمهور العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars explain God's “mocking” as naming punishment after the sin, a common Arabic usage illustrated by ʿAmr b. Kulthūm's retaliatory verse.
rows.anchor: هي تسمية العقوبة باسم الذنب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḥasan are associated with reports of acts that seem like mockery to human observers: Hell's fire congeals like tallow, luring them before it collapses, and its doors appear to open for escape.
rows.anchor: أن النار تجمد كما تجمد الإهالة

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others explain the mockery as gradual enticement: worldly blessings make them think God approves, though their punishment is already decreed, which looks like mockery from a human perspective.
rows.anchor: استدراجهم من حيث لا يعلمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yamduduhum means that God increases them in transgression; Mujāhid instead glosses it as giving them respite.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: «معناه يملي لهم»

rows.speaker: يونس بن حبيب
rows.claim: Yūnus says madd is used for extension in evil, while amadda is used for good.
rows.anchor: يقال مد في الشر وأمد في الخير

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another linguistic account distinguishes extension by something of the same kind (madda) from supplementation by a different kind (amadda), illustrated by a river enlarged by another river.
rows.anchor: مد الشيء ومده ما كان مثله ومن جنسه

rows.speaker: اللحياني
rows.claim: Al-Liḥyānī says adding more of the same kind is madd; Qurʾān 31:27 says the sea is extended by seven more seas, and mādda names what extends a thing.
rows.anchor: والبحر يمده من بعده سبعة أبحر

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba and others treat maddadtu al-dawāt and amdadtuha (“I supplied the inkwell”) as equivalent; Ibn ʿAṭiyya tentatively distinguishes adding ink from making it supplied with ink.
rows.anchor: ابن قتيبة وغيره: «مددت الدواة وأمددتها بمعنى»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He allows “extend them in transgression” to mean either prolong and defer them, as in “extended pillars” (104:9), or increase transgression itself; ṭughyān is excess beyond bounds.
rows.anchor: فتحتمل اللفظة أن تكون من المد الذي هو المطل والتطويل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʿmahūn means wandering in perplexity; ʿamah is confusion in sight or judgment, as one lost in darkness or desert seems unable to see.
rows.anchor: ويعمهون يترددون حيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awlāʾika begins a nominal sentence, alladhīna is its predicate, and ishtaraw is the relative clause; the verb is morphologically explained from ishtariyū through vowel change and deletion.
rows.anchor: أولئك إشارة إلى المتقدم ذكرهم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī says ḍamma on the plural wāw in ishtaraw helps distinguish it from wāw in aw or law, whose vowels are kasra.
rows.anchor: الضم فيها أولى ليفصل بينها وبين واو

rows.speaker: أبو السمال قعنب العدوي
rows.claim: Abū al-Sammāl Qunb reads ishtaraw with fatḥa on wāw.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو السمال قعنب العدوي بفتح الواو

rows.speaker: يحيى بن يعمر
rows.claim: Yaḥyā b. Yaʿmar reads ishtaraw with kasra on wāw.
rows.anchor: وقرأها يحيى بن يعمر بكسر الواو

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some gloss “they purchased misguidance for guidance” as taking misguidance and abandoning guidance; others say they preferred misguidance and shunned guidance, as in 41:17.
rows.anchor: استحبوا الضلالة وتجنبوا الهدى

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others take purchase as a metaphor: guidance was available but they chose misguidance in its place, as if they paid their guidance for it.
rows.anchor: شبهوا بمن اشترى فكأنهم دفعوا في الضلالة هداهم

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik invokes the metaphor to bar a purchase option over items of one kind whose individual units differ and cannot lawfully be exchanged unequally.
rows.anchor: تعلق مالك رحمه الله في منع أن يشتري الرجل

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say the verse concerns a hypocrite who once believed, then inwardly apostatized; on this reading the transaction is nearly literal.
rows.anchor: فيمن كان آمن من المنافقين ثم ارتد في باطنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Their trade did not profit” closes the parable by echoing its opening image of purchase; profit is attributed to the trade, as in Arabic expressions “a standing night” and “a fasting day.”
rows.anchor: ختم للمثل بما يشبه مبدأه في لفظة الشراء

rows.speaker: إبراهيم بن أبي عبلة
rows.claim: Ibrāhīm b. Abī ʿAbla reads “their trades” in the plural.
rows.anchor: فما ربحت تجاراتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “They were not guided” may refer to this transaction, be a general description, or refer to God's prior knowledge; the wording permits all three.
rows.anchor: وما كانوا مهتدين قيل المعنى في شرائهم هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naqḍ is undoing something firmly tied so it returns to its original unbound state; ʿahd here is a prior commitment or injunction.
rows.anchor: النقض رد ما أبرم على أوله غير مبرم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: One interpretation identifies the covenant as God's primordial covenant with Adam's descendants, drawn out like particles from his back.
rows.anchor: أخذه الله على بني آدم حين استخرجهم من ظهر أبيهم آدم

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another interpretation calls the signs of God's oneness in the heavens, earth, and created order themselves a covenant.
rows.anchor: نصب الأدلة على وحدانية الله بالسماوات والأرض

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: A further view makes the covenant transmitted through messengers: worship God alone and worship no other.
rows.anchor: بواسطة رسله أن يوحدوه وأن لا يعبدوا غيره

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others identify the covenant of scriptural communities as belief in Muḥammad and not concealing his status; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this specifically concerns the People of the Book, though surrounding context concerns all disbelievers.
rows.anchor: محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم، وأن لا يكتموا أمره

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the verse is about people who believed in the Prophet and then disbelieved, thereby breaking their covenant.
rows.anchor: هذه الآية هي فيمن كان آمن بالنبي عليه السلام ثم كفر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī did not attribute these interpretations; any covenant made lawfully among Muslims may not be broken under this verse. The pronoun in mīthāqihi can refer to the covenant or to God's name.
rows.anchor: وكل عهد جائز بين المسلمين فنقضه لا يحل بهذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mīthāq is a noun for the act of binding, from wathāqa; the verse uses it as a verbal noun, as in ʿAmr b. Shayyim's line meaning “after your giving.”
rows.anchor: وهو في هذه الآية اسم في موضع المصدر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda understands the thing severed as kinship generally among people; another view narrows it to kinship between believers and says disbelievers severed ties with those who followed Muḥammad.
rows.anchor: الأرحام عامة في الناس

rows.speaker: جمهور أهل العلم
rows.claim: Most scholars say the connection to be maintained is God's religion and worship on earth, observance of its laws, and preservation of its limits.
rows.anchor: الإشارة في هذه الآية إلى دين الله وعبادته في الأرض

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو محمد
rows.claim: He endorses the majority interpretation of maintaining God's religion and says kinship is one part of it; the clause with an is accusative as an appositive to mā or as purpose, with a genitive appositional analysis also possible.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو الحق، والرحم جزء من هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Corruption on earth means worshiping other than God and acting unjustly according to desires; loss is depriving oneself of a share in success and triumph.
rows.anchor: يفسدون في الأرض يعبدون غير الله ويجورون في الأفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How can you disbelieve?” is not a real question but a statement of reproach and reminder of God's blessings and power; grammatically kayfa is a circumstantial adverb modifying the disbelief.
rows.anchor: لفظه الاستفهام وليس به، بل هو تقرير وتوبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question may also convey astonishment at the strangeness of rejecting a benefactor; wāw in “while you were dead” marks a circumstantial clause.
rows.anchor: ومن قال إن كيف تقرير وتعجب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن مسعود ومجاهد
rows.claim: They say people were nonexistent before creation, were brought to earthly life, then underwent ordinary death and will be raised at the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: كنتم أمواتا معدومين قبل أن تخلقوا

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another account begins with Adam as lifeless clay, then his enlivening by the spirit, followed by human death and resurrection.
rows.anchor: كنتم أمواتا بكون آدم من طين ميتا قبل أن يحيى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda interprets the first death as the descendants' existence in their fathers' loins before being brought into the world.
rows.anchor: كنتم أمواتا في أصلاب آبائكم

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another view says people were dead in the womb before ensoulment, then were brought to earthly life, died, and will be raised.
rows.anchor: كنتم أمواتا في الأرحام قبل نفخ الروح

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God brought forth human souls as particles, then caused them to die; He later gave them worldly life, followed by death and Resurrection.
rows.anchor: أخرج نسم بني آدم أمثال الذر ثم أماتهم بعد ذلك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو صالح
rows.claim: They say people die the familiar death, are revived for questioning in the graves, die there, then are revived for the Resurrection.
rows.anchor: ثم أحياكم للسؤال في القبور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A further report from Ibn ʿAbbās takes death as obscurity and lack of renown, then life as being honored and remembered through this religion and its Prophet.
rows.anchor: كنتم أمواتا بالخمول فأحياكم بأن ذكرتم وشرفتم بهذا الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thumma orders the presentation of statements, not events themselves. One view says istawā means rose without specifying how or delimiting God; al-Ṭabarī prefers this, glossing it as the rule of His command, power, and dominion.
rows.anchor: معناه علا دون تكييف ولا تحديد

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysān glosses istawā as turning toward heaven; Ibn ʿAṭiyya specifies that this means turning to create and originate it.
rows.anchor: معناه قصد إلى السماء

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say God completed heaven's construction, but Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls that interpretation strained; al-Ṭabarī also reports “turned toward” as a weak option.
rows.anchor: القاضي أبو محمد: وهذا قلق

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: The report that the subject of “the one who rose” is smoke conflicts with the wording's arrangement, while interpreting istawā as “conquered” fits 20:5 better; here one retains God's power and dominion without movement or created change.
rows.anchor: والقاعدة في هذه الآية ونحوها منع النقلة وحلول الحوادث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fasawwāhunna can mean making the heavens equal or smoothing their surfaces; sabʿa may be apposition, object with an understood preposition, or circumstantial, and al-samāʾ can be plural or a collective singular.
rows.anchor: فسواهن قيل المعنى جعلهن سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's knowledge encompasses existing things; knowledge of nonexistents is established by other verses. Earth was created before heaven, then spread out afterward, reconciling this verse with passages in al-Muʾmin and al-Nāziʿāt.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية تقتضي أن الأرض وما فيها خلق قبل السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Man is the subject and yarghabu its predicate; raghiba ʿan means to turn away from or disdain the religion of Abraham, where milla means a revealed law or way.
rows.anchor: والمعنى يزهد فيها ويربأ بنفسه عنها

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj takes safiha as “was ignorant” and says its transitivity here follows its meaning.
rows.anchor: سفه بمعنى جهل وعداه بالمعنى

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another grammatical account says safiha means “destroyed”; Thalab and al-Mubarrad also report a kasra form, which Abū al-Khaṭṭāb says is dialectal.
rows.anchor: سفه بمعنى أهلك

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ parses nafsahu as a specification (tamyīz); Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains that foolishness can characterize the self, judgment, or character but notes the pronoun's prior ambiguity weakens that analysis.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء نصبها على التمييز

rows.speaker: البصريون
rows.claim: The Basrans reject a specification with this definite form and instead posit omitted fī (“in himself”), which strengthens the verb; Makkī's analysis as an emphatic substitute is called strained by Ibn ʿAṭiyya.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز التمييز مع هذا التعريف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iṣṭafā is an iftaʿala form from ṣafwa, meaning to choose the purest; tāʾ changes to ṭāʾ to match ṣād in emphatic articulation, and Abraham's election means God made him a prophet and intimate friend.
rows.anchor: ومعنى هذا الاصطفاء أنه نبأه واتخذه خليلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In the Hereafter” cannot modify al-ṣāliḥīn if al- is relative because a relative cannot precede its clause; alternatives make al- definite or supply an omitted noun such as “in the deeds of the Hereafter.”
rows.anchor: لأن الصلة لا تتقدم الموصول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “when his Lord said to him, Submit” modifies God's choosing Abraham; this command came when Abraham was tested by the star, moon, and sun. Islam here is its fullest form.
rows.anchor: وكان هذا القول من الله حين ابتلاه بالكوكب والقمر والشمس

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read awṣā (“enjoined”) instead of waṣṣā; both mean the same, though waṣṣā suggests repeated or emphatic instruction.
rows.anchor: نافع وابن عامر «وأوصى» ، وقرأ الباقون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “with it” may refer to Abraham's statement “I submit to the Lord of the worlds” or the preceding religion; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the nearer statement.
rows.anchor: والأول أصوب لأنه أقرب مذكور

rows.speaker: عمرو بن فائد الأسواري
rows.claim: ʿAmr b. Fāʾid reads Yaʿqūb in the accusative, including Jacob among those who enjoined their children; other grammarians coordinate him with Abraham or treat him separately as saying “My sons.”
rows.anchor: عمرو بن فائد الأسواري «ويعقوب» بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iṣṭafā here means choosing the purest religions; al-dīn refers to the already known religion. Inna is kasra after waṣṣā because it represents quoted speech, and Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read an yā banī with an explicit particle.
rows.anchor: الألف واللام في الدين للعهد، لأنهم قد كانوا عرفوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not die except as Muslims” concisely commands Islam and perseverance: since one knows death will come but not when, one must remain constantly upon the command. Antum muslimūn is a circumstantial nominal clause.
rows.anchor: فإذا أمر بأمر لا يأتيه الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address rebukes Jews and Christians claiming the prophets for their own religions: Jacob and the earlier prophets followed pure monotheism and submission, so the claimants lack eyewitness knowledge and are inventing their claim.
rows.anchor: هذا الخطاب لليهود والنصارى الذين انتحلوا الأنبياء

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some take am as “rather”: the ancestors witnessed Jacob and learned his testament but rejected it and falsely attributed another religion to him; Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds “rather” plus an interrogative hamza the strongest reading.
rows.anchor: والأظهر أنها التي بمعنى بل وألف الاستفهام معا

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says am can pose a question in the middle of discourse after an earlier opening, as in examples such as “Or do they say he invented it?”
rows.anchor: وحكى الطبري أن أم يستفهم بها في وسط كلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuhadāʾ means witnesses who were present; Jacob's “death came” means its preliminaries, since a person at the instant of death could not speak. Jacob is placed first because he is the focus; the second id-clause apposes the first.
rows.anchor: لو حضر الموت لما أمكن أن يقول شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob asks what they will worship as a test; using “what” rather than “whom” avoids opening a path to their claim, and common objects of worship include idols, fire, sun, and stones.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل من لئلا يطرق لهم الاهتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Jacob chose death, asked for time to advise his family, and gathered his sons, who affirmed their faith and knowledge of God; “after me” means after his death.
rows.anchor: وقال أمهلوني حتى أوصي بني وأهلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ismāʿīl is included among Jacob's fathers because he was his uncle.
rows.anchor: ودخل إسماعيل في الآباء لأنه عم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet asked that al-ʿAbbās be returned to him, fearing Quraysh would treat him as Thaqīf had treated ʿUrwa b. Masʿūd; elsewhere he called him a remnant of his forefathers and said “I am the son of the two sacrificed,” on the well-known view that Isaac was the sacrifice.
rows.anchor: هذا بقية آبائي

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن يعمر والجحدري وأبو رجاء
rows.claim: They read “and the god of your father” in the singular; it may mean Abraham alone, though some parse abī as a sound masculine plural, attested by Sībawayh and Ziyād b. Wāṣil's verse.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وابن يعمر والجحدري وأبو رجاء «وإله أبيك»

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says Ismāʿīl is named before Isaac because he was older.
rows.anchor: يقال قدم إسماعيل لأنه أسن من إسحاق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilāhan may be an appositive repeating “your God” to add the quality of oneness, or a circumstantial accusative; Ibn ʿAṭiyya favors the latter because the point is to establish the state of unity. “We submit to Him” is more laudatory as a complete clause than as a circumstantial phrase.
rows.anchor: لأن الغرض إثبات حال الوحدانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The departed community is the prophets mentioned; Jewish and Christian claimants cannot benefit from their ancestors' good deeds, since each person has earned good or evil, and the verse refutes the Jabriyya denial of human acquisition.
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الآية رد على الجبرية القائلين لا اكتساب للعبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You will not be asked about their deeds” rejects inheriting their religion. The claim that only Jews or Christians attain guidance echoes 2:111; milla is accusative after an omitted “we follow” or as an exhortation, while the raised reading means “rather, guidance is a religion.”
rows.anchor: نظير قولهم لن يدخل الجنة إلا من كان هودا أو نصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanīf usually means one who turns away from rejected religions toward truth; some say it means upright obedience, a pilgrim, or circumcised. The author explains the term through turning or inclination, with “straightness” also reported.
rows.anchor: الأحنف لمن مالت إحدى قدميه إلى الأخرى

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some commentators say ḥanaf means uprightness; they associate the name al-aḥnaf for crooked feet with hopeful naming.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: الحنف الاستقامة، وسمي المعوج القدمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators narrow ḥanīf to a pilgrim or to a circumcised person, but these are only particular aspects of the broader sense of turning toward true religion.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: المختتن، وهذه أجزاء الحنف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's disavowal of association with God excludes idol worship and the Jewish and Christian claims that Ezra or the Messiah is God's son.
rows.anchor: والنصرانية لقولهم المسيح ابن الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Choosing misguidance after rejecting accessible guidance is pictured as trade; punishment follows the chosen error and forgiveness would have followed the guidance they discarded, so both are included in the metaphorical purchase.
rows.anchor: ولما كان العذاب تابعا للضلالة التي اشتروها

rows.speaker: جمهور المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes take mā aṣbarahum as an exclamation: they are astonishingly fit to remain long in the Fire, as in 80:17 and 19:38.
rows.anchor: وهو في حيز المخاطبين، أي هم أهل أن تعجبوا منهم

rows.speaker: قتادة والحسن وابن جبير والربيع
rows.claim: They explain the exclamation as amazement at the hypocrites' audacity: their behavior shows they have prepared themselves for the Fire and are willing to enter it.
rows.anchor: أظهر التعجب من صبرهم على النار لما عملوا عمل من وطن نفسه عليها

rows.speaker: معمر بن المثنى
rows.claim: Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā reads mā as an interrogative: what has made them endure the Fire? Ibn ʿAṭiyya considers the exclamatory reading clearer.
rows.anchor: استفهام معناه أي شيء أصبرهم على النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aṣbara can mean commanding someone to be patient or making someone patient; either sense works if the clause is interrogative.
rows.anchor: ومعنى أصبرهم في اللغة أمرهم بالصبر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad calls the phrase an interrogative report, not an exclamation, and parses aṣbara as “confined or forced,” citing the prohibition on tormenting a living creature and a poetic line.
rows.anchor: الضبط عند المبرد بضم الهمزة وكسر الباء

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو محمد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says al-Mubarrad's vowel analysis is wrong: the poetic form is aṣbarahā with fatḥa on hamza and ḍamma on bāʾ, past tense of ṣabara; this undercuts the proposed “make patient” sense.
rows.anchor: الضبط عند المبرد بضم الهمزة وكسر الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That is because God sent down the Book in truth” may mean the Fire became due because they disbelieved it; several implied clauses are possible, and the Book can mean the Qurʾān as a whole.
rows.anchor: المعنى ذلك الأمر أو الأمر ذلك بأن الله نزل الكتاب بالحق

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Another reading connects “the Book” with the earlier statement that unbelievers are not affected by warning (2:6): their punishment was established by the Book's report, or their purchase of misguidance followed God's prior knowledge and report.
rows.anchor: إن الإشارة ب الكتاب إلى قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq can mean what is obligatory or what is true in the reports; shiqāq is opposition that tears the bond between adversaries, and baʿīd means far from truth and uprightness.
rows.anchor: وبعيد هنا معناه من الحق والاستقامة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī identifies those who differed over the Book as Jews and Christians, each forming a separate opposing camp.
rows.anchor: هم اليهود والنصارى لأن هؤلاء في شق وهؤلاء في شق

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others identify the disputants as Arab disbelievers who called the Qurʾān magic, legends, or fabrication; their conflict is with Islam and its adherents.
rows.anchor: المراد ب الذين اختلفوا كفار العرب لقول بعضهم هو سحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next clause begins the discussion that piety is not merely turning toward east or west; the reading with rafʿ makes al-birr the subject of laysa.
rows.anchor: قرأ أكثر السبعة برفع الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shuhh meant in the linked report is the inborn acquisitive impulse, as in 4:128, not the blameworthy greed of miserliness; dhawī al-qurbā means blood relatives.
rows.anchor: والشح في هذا الحديث هو الغريزي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An orphan is a human child who has lost his father before maturity.
rows.anchor: واليتم في الآدميين من قبل الأب قبل البلوغ

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and others define the wayfarer as a traveler, because he stays closely attached to the road; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this reading is broader than Qatāda's alternative, “a guest.”
rows.anchor: ابن السبيل المسافر لملازمته السبيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression is like calling a bird that stays by water “son of water”; the Prophet's phrase “son of fornication” similarly means one associated with it. Another derivation likens a road's traveler to something born from the road.
rows.anchor: وهذا كما يقال ابن ماء للطائر الملازم للماء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda takes ibn al-sabīl to mean a guest; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the more general traveler interpretation.
rows.anchor: والأول أعم، وفي الرقاب: يراد به العتق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In the necks” covers freeing slaves, releasing captives, and helping pay the final installments of emancipation contracts; prayer is performed with all its conditions, and naming zakāt here distinguishes the earlier giving from obligatory zakāt.
rows.anchor: يراد به العتق وفك الأسرى وإعطاء أواخر الكتابات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mūfūn can coordinate with “who believe” or begin an implied “they are the faithful”; al-ṣābirīn is accusative for praise or after an understood verb. Ibn Masʿūd's codex has al-mūfīn, while Yaʿqūb, al-Aʿmash, and al-Ḥasan read both descriptors in nominative; al-Jaḥdarī reads “their covenants.”
rows.anchor: عبد الله بن مسعود «والموفين» على المدح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-baʾsāʾ means poverty, al-ḍarrāʾ illness or bodily calamity, and ḥīna al-baʾs the time of fierce fighting; Arabic usage also distinguishes poverty from courage with related forms.
rows.anchor: والبأساء الفقر والفاقة، والضراء المرض ومصائب البدن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God calls the people who practice these virtues truthful because they fulfill the hopes placed in them, as in “wealth proved true for me”; truthfulness may also refer to truthful speech. Their piety is a shield from punishment made by good works.
rows.anchor: ثم وصف تعالى أهل هذه الأفعال البرة بالصدق في أمورهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barazū means they emerged onto open, spacious ground; Jālūt is a non-Arabic name adapted into Arabic, and ifrāgh is a full and ample pouring-out of patience.
rows.anchor: صاروا في البراز وهو الأفيح من الأرض المتسع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image of making feet firm evokes stability; the root of defeat means striking something so its parts fold into one another, then came to mean an army's defeat and retreat.
rows.anchor: والهزم أصله أن يضرب الشيء فيدخل بعضه في بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jālūt was king and commander of the ʿAmālīq; a report numbers his force at three hundred thousand horsemen.
rows.anchor: وكان فيما روي في ثلاثمائة ألف فارس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A narrative says David's brothers, sons of Īshā, served Ṭālūt while young David tended his father's sheep; on the way to see the battle, stones called to him, saying one of them would enable him to kill Jālūt, and he took them.
rows.anchor: مر في طريقه بحجر فناداه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jālūt challenged the fighters, but everyone held back; Ṭālūt offered his daughter and wealth to whoever killed him, and David volunteered. After borrowing armor and a horse, David returned to fight in his usual way, trusting God rather than equipment.
rows.anchor: إن الله إن لم يقتله لي ويعني عليه لم ينفعني هذا الفرس ولا هذا السلاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story continues that David, expert with a sling, confronted armored Jālūt; a stone or joined stones struck his head after David invoked God, and David killed and beheaded him, routing the enemy.
rows.anchor: وكان داود من أرمى الناس بالمقلاع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭālūt demanded that David kill two hundred oppressors, the Garājima, and bring their foreskins, hoping he would die; David succeeded and received the king's daughter.
rows.anchor: ولا بد لك من قتل مائتين من هؤلاء الجراجمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports disagree whether Ṭālūt yielded the kingdom to David, Israel made David king because he killed Jālūt, or Ṭālūt pursued him until his death and Israel then appointed David; a report says Samuel anointed him at God's direction after examining Īshā's sons.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن بني إسرائيل غلبت طالوت على ذلك بسبب أن داود قتل جالوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reports on this story have weak chains; Ibn ʿAṭiyya selects only what explains the verse and the sequence of events, while the verse itself establishes that David became king of Israel.
rows.anchor: وقد أكثر الناس في قصص هذه الآية، وذلك كله لين الأسانيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wisdom given David was prophecy and the Psalms; his knowledge included armor-making, the speech of birds, and other sciences.
rows.anchor: وأما الحكمة التي آتاه الله فهي النبوة والزبور

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī says David received Ṭālūt's kingdom and the prophethood of Shimʿūn.
rows.anchor: آتاه الله ملك طالوت ونبوة شمعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God says that without His sending believers against disbelievers through the ages, disbelief would engulf the earth; He always leaves someone upholding truth, calling to God, and fighting for it, now in Muḥammad's community until the Hour.
rows.anchor: لولا دفعه بالمؤمنين في صدور الكفرة على مر الدهر لفسدت الأرض

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: Makkī says most commentators understand that God protects non-prayers through those who pray and the heedless through those who fear Him, otherwise destroying people for their sins; Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects this as unrelated to the verse.
rows.anchor: لولا أن الله يدفع بمن يصلي عمن لا يصلي

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو محمد
rows.claim: Although Ibn ʿUmar's hadith is sound, Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects Makkī's claim that Ibn ʿUmar supported that reading with this verse, judging Ibn ʿUmar too eloquent to have done so.
rows.anchor: والحديث الذي رواه ابن عمر صحيح

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وابن كثير
rows.claim: They read “wa-lawlā dafʿu Allāh” here and “inna Allāha yudāfiʿu” in 22:38; Nāfiʿ reads difāʿ in both, while the remaining readers use dafʿ here and yudāfiʿu there.
rows.anchor: أبو عمرو وابن كثير: ولولا دفع الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Difāʿ can be the verbal noun of dafaʿa, like kitāb from kataba, or of dāfaʿa, like qitāl from qātala.
rows.anchor: والدفاع يحتمل أن يكون مصدر دفع ككتب كتابا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the debt-documentation verse was revealed specifically concerning forward sales (salam); Ibn ʿAṭiyya says such sales in Medina occasioned it, but the rule covers all debts by consensus.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنه نزلت هذه الآية في السلم خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding “with a debt” disambiguates tadaayantum, since Arabic can use it for mutual repayment; an expressly specified term rules out an unknown maturity date.
rows.anchor: ووصفه الأجل بمسمى دليل على أن المجهلة لا تجوز

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ says documentation was initially made obligatory by the command, then lightened by the trust exception in 2:283.
rows.anchor: ثم خففه الله تعالى بقوله

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbī, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd report the view that “if one of you trusts another” abrogates the documentation command; a report attributes the position to Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي: كانوا يرون أن

rows.speaker: جمهور العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars treat writing as recommended protection of property and removal of doubt; it does not harm a pious debtor and protects the creditor against an unreliable one.
rows.anchor: الأمر بالكتب ندب إلى حفظ الأموال وإزالة الريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sound view is that witnessing makes a transaction prudent while mutual trust leaves room; no abrogation follows, because documentation is recommended as a precaution for rights people may waive, and 2:283 instructs debtors to repay when trusted.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو القول الصحيح

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī treats documentation as obligatory and argues that commands remain obligatory until evidence shows otherwise.
rows.anchor: ذهب إلى أن الأمر بالكتب فرض واجب

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAṭāʾ and others say “let a scribe write” makes writing obligatory on the scribe; al-Shaʿbī and ʿAṭāʾ also specify that this applies when he is the only available scribe, while al-Suddī says it applies when he is free.
rows.anchor: واجب على الكاتب أن يكتب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “With justice” modifies the act of writing, not the noun “scribe”; a child, slave, or disfavored person can draft a sound document, though officials should use upright, trusted, knowledgeable document writers.
rows.anchor: والباء متعلقة بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik says only someone knowledgeable about documents, personally upright and trusted, should write them, citing the command to write justly.
rows.anchor: لا يكتب الوثائق من الناس إلا عارف بها عدل في نفسه مأمون

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The verb abā yaʾbā is irregular: among verbs with a fatḥa in the imperfect, this pattern normally occurs only when a guttural letter is involved; al-Zajjāj says the hamza resembles one.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج والقول في أبى أن الألف فيه أشبهت الهمزة

rows.speaker: الربيع والضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Rabīʿ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, as transmitted by al-Mahdawī, say the prohibition on a scribe refusing was abrogated by the command not to cause harm in 2:282.
rows.anchor: أن قوله ولا يأب منسوخ بقوله لا يضار كاتب ولا شهيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As Allah taught him can attach to “write” as the manner of writing, to “not refuse” as a reason to repay God's gift, or begin a new sentence that attaches to “let him write.”
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون كما متعلقة بما في قوله ولا يأب من المعنى

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو محمد
rows.claim: No particular scribe must write if another is available, and he may decline unless hired; if none is available, an exhortatory duty falls on the present person. Documentation in general is recommended, like doing good in 22:77, and helps someone in need.
rows.anchor: وأما الكتب في الجملة فندب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because documentation can be burdensome, God removes blame for leaving immediate cash transactions unwritten; such dealings are usually small purchases rather than property. Al-Suddī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk define them as immediate hand-to-hand exchange.
rows.anchor: هذا فيما كان يدا بيد تأخذ وتعطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An is accusative as a disconnected exception. “You turn it over between yourselves” implies possession transfers; land, houses, and much livestock cannot be handed over cleanly in the same way, so debt-like documentation suits them.
rows.anchor: تديرونها بينكم يقتضي التقابض والبينونة بالمقبوض

rows.speaker: عاصم
rows.claim: ʿĀṣim reads tijāratan in the accusative; the other readers read it in the nominative, though Abū ʿAlī is unsure about Ibn ʿĀmir.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عاصم وحده «تجارة» نصبا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With nominative, kāna means “occur” and needs no predicate; with accusative, its event sense is absent and an omitted subject or predicate is supplied, such as “unless the transaction is a trade.”
rows.anchor: فحجة من رفع تجارة إن كان بمعنى حدث ووقع

rows.speaker: أبو علي والمبرد
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī and al-Mubarrad transmit a poetic line with “if it were an awful day” using accusative yawm; al-Ṭabarī's variant has nominative, as does Sībawayh's version.
rows.anchor: وأنشده سيبويه بالرفع إذا كان يوم ذو كواكب

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī interprets “witness when you transact” as applying to transactions both small and large.
rows.anchor: وأشهدوا على صغير ذلك وكبيره

rows.speaker: الحسن والشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, al-Shaʿbī, and others say witnessing a transaction is recommended; Ibn ʿAmr and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say it is obligatory, followed by Ibn ʿUmar's practice and ʿAṭāʾ, with al-Ṭabarī preferring obligation.
rows.anchor: ذلك على الندب

rows.speaker: القاضي أبو محمد
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds obligation untenable: witnessing tiny sales is burdensome, while larger dealings may rely on social trust or customary practice. He prefers recommendation unless an excuse prevents it.
rows.anchor: والوجوب في ذلك قلق أما في الدقائق فصعب شاق

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some say witnessing is abrogated by the trust exception in 2:283; al-Mahdawī records this view and Makkī attributes it to Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī.
rows.anchor: وأشهدوا إذا تبايعتم منسوخ بقوله فإن أمن

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وطاوس وابن زيد
rows.claim: They say “do not harm a scribe or witness” prohibits a writer from adding to or subtracting from what was dictated and a witness from altering testimony; Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and ʿAṭāʾ also understand it to prohibit their refusal.
rows.anchor: ولا يضار الكاتب بأن يكتب ما لم يمل عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والضحاك والسدي وطاوس
rows.claim: They say a claimant harms a scribe or witness by demanding work when that person is busy or excused, then shaming him for refusing; the word's reciprocal sense encompasses these readings and the preceding ones.
rows.anchor: بأن يؤذيه طالب الكتبة أو الشهادة فيقول اكتب لي

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب وابن مسعود ومجاهد
rows.claim: They read the verb with the letters separated and the first rāʾ fatḥa, meaning a claimant may initiate harm to the scribe or witness; al-Ṭabarī reports and explains this reading accordingly.
rows.anchor: كانوا يقرؤون «ولا يضارر» بالفك وفتح الراء الأولى

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو الداني
rows.claim: Al-Dānī reports both kasra and fatḥa for the first rāʾ from ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, and Mujāhid; separating the consonants is Ḥijāzī usage, while assimilation is Tamīmī.
rows.anchor: وفك الفعل هي لغة أهل الحجاز والإدغام لغة تميم

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر بن القعقاع وعمرو بن عبيد
rows.claim: They read the geminated rāʾ with sukūn in the jussive; Abū al-Fatḥ calls it questionable but explains it as treating connected speech like a pause.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر بن القعقاع وعمرو بن عبيد «ولا يضار» بجزم الراء

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima reads the first rāʾ with kasra and makes “scribe” and “witness” accusative, so that the rights-holder is forbidden to begin harming them.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عكرمة «ولا يضارر» بكسر الراء الأولى

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin reads the geminated verb with rafʿ; after Ibn Mujāhid questions it, Abū al-Fatḥ explains it as a negative statement meaning the scribe ought not to be harmed, supported by poetry. Ibn ʿAṭiyya finds it close to the earlier analysis.
rows.anchor: ولا أدري ما هذه القراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If harm means falsification by a writer or witness, fisq is the legal commission of grave sins and invalidating rights; if it means mistreatment or refusal, fisq means departing from what is right, though disobeying God's command approaches the legal sense too.
rows.anchor: فالفسوق على عرفه في الشرع وهو مواقعة الكبائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bikum implies “a state of fisq upon you”; the close of the verse admonishes and recounts God's favor, and another interpretation promises that piety teaches a person what is good.
rows.anchor: وقيل إن معنى الآية الوعد بأن من اتقى علم الخير وألهمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After recommending documentation and witnessing, the verse addresses circumstances preventing writing and substitutes a pledged security; travel is the common case, but other impediments, including a debtor's unreliable standing, also justify a pledge.
rows.anchor: وجعل لها الرهن ونص من أحوال العذر على السفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet pledged his armor to a Jewish seller who lent him barley; when the seller alleged he meant to take his money, the Prophet swore he was trustworthy in heaven and earth and said he would repay if entrusted.
rows.anchor: وقد رهن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم درعه عند يهودي

rows.speaker: جمهور من العلماء
rows.claim: Most scholars say the Qurʾān establishes pledges in travel, while the Prophetic report establishes them at home; Ibn ʿAṭiyya agrees but says the verse's travel scenario is only an example, so its general meaning includes home circumstances.
rows.anchor: فالرهن في الحضر موجود في الآية بالمعنى

rows.speaker: الضحاك ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Mujāhid confine both pledges and trust to travel; al-Ṭabarī weakens their restriction on pledges because of the sound hadith but supports their restriction on trust. Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects both limits, saying trust is common and sound at home too.
rows.anchor: والصحيح ضعف القول في الفصلين بل يقع الائتمان في الحضر كثيرا

rows.speaker: جمهور القراء
rows.claim: Most readers have kātiban, “a writer”; Ubayy b. Kaʿb and Ibn ʿAbbās read kitāban, a verbal noun or a plural of writer, and Mujāhid and Abū al-ʿĀliya explain it as absence of writing tools or supplies. Ibn ʿAbbās also has a plural reading for writers, and Abū al-ʿĀliya reads kutuban, books; Ibn ʿAṭiyya accepts the readings except insofar as the consonantal text favors one.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي بن كعب وابن عباس «كتابا» بكسر الكاف

rows.speaker: نافع وعاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: They and most scholars read rihān; Abū ʿAmr and Ibn Kathīr read ruhun, sometimes with a lightened hāʾ, and groups read both forms.
rows.anchor: نافع وعاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي وجمهور من العلماء «فرهان»

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahn in Arabic can mean to remain or continue; a poem's “meat and bread are lasting” illustrates the sense. Jurists consequently void a pledge when it leaves the creditor's possession, since it departs from its defining state.
rows.anchor: رهن الشيء في كلام العرب معناه: دام واستمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arhana can mean to bid heavily for an item until obtaining it at a high price, illustrated by a poem about a noble she-camel for which dinars were paid.
rows.anchor: ويقال أرهن في السلعة إذا غالى فيها حتى أخذها بكثير الثمن

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Some attest arhantu irhānan for collateral, while Abū ʿAlī distinguishes arhantu for outbidding from rahantu for loan or sale; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says rahantu rahnan is standard without disagreement, with the verbal noun transferred to the pledged object and treated as a noun.
rows.anchor: بلا خلاف في البيع والقرض: رهنت رهنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pledge noun's plural takes kasra like nouns and lexicalized verbal nouns; in “I pledged a garment,” the verb takes an object rather than an internal verbal noun. Abū ʿAlī nevertheless allows arhantu, though rahantu is more frequent.
rows.anchor: صار فعله ينصبه نصب المفعول به لا نصب المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic examples from al-Aʿshā and Hammām b. Murra attest forms from both rahana and arhāna in the pledge sense.
rows.anchor: فهذه رويت من رهن وأما أرهن فمنه قول همام بن مرة
